about: Implementation 04-3, Phase 2: the gallery of patterns. One pattern, one name: Phase 3 uses these ids and levels in the level prompts. Images are relative to this folder (drawn/) or to context/implementations/04-app-enhancements/images/chopin_passages/. pdf pages are pages of the user's PDFs in /home/david/Documents/projects/music/chopin/ (outside the repo). kern files are in poc-aitu-research/data/raw/kern/humdrum-chopin-first-editions/kern/.

patterns.name: Slow melody in single notes
patterns.line: Si4 held for three beats, then Do5: the melody alone, with long notes and no chords. Easy because the hand has one note at a time and almost no movement.

examples.note: Long notes over a left hand that moves a lot: the right hand still stays in one place.

patterns.name: Melody in single notes
patterns.line: Fa#5-Sol5-Fa#5-Do#5-Re5-Si4 in corcheas, then La#4: one line of single notes inside one hand position. Easy because there are no chords, also when the notes are corcheas.

examples.note: A line that goes down by steps.

patterns.name: Chords in one position
patterns.line: Two- and three-note chords with the melody on top, all inside one octava, while the left hand runs. Easy because the hand does not move, although every note is a chord.

patterns.name: Repeated note with chords
patterns.line: One note repeated in corcheas, with a chord below it on the strong beats (the repeated note of Prelude 15, now in the right hand). Easy because the hand stays on the same keys.

patterns.name: Repeated two-note chord
patterns.line: The same third played again in negras, with one note changing now and then. Easy because two fingers stay on two keys.

patterns.name: Five-finger melody
patterns.line: The melody inside five keys (Mi4 to Do5) in negras and blancas. Easy because each finger has its key and the hand never moves.

patterns.name: Chords on each beat
patterns.line: The triad of the harmony on every negra (Fa4-La4-Do5, Mi4-Sol4-Do5, Fa4-Sib4-Re5). Easy because the chord changes only with the harmony and stays in one place.

patterns.name: Repeated chord in corcheas
patterns.line: The same triad played again in corcheas. Easy because the hand keeps one shape; only the speed asks something.

patterns.name: Two-note chords in one position
patterns.line: Fa4-La4, then La4-Do5, in negras: two notes of the triad, then the two above them. Easy because the hand does not move.

patterns.name: Broken triad in one position
patterns.line: Fa4-Do5-La4-Do5 in corcheas (an Alberti figure in the right hand). Easy because the three fingers stay on the three keys of the chord.

patterns.name: A second note on long notes
patterns.line: Single notes on the short figures, and a second note (a third, a sixth) only on the long ones; three notes only to land on a long note. Medium because the hand stays fluent and the chords come when there is time for them.

examples.note: Sol#4-Mi5 held as a sixth, then Fa##4-Re#5.

examples.piece: Ballade No. 1 in G minor, Op. 23
examples.note: Two notes on the blancas with puntillo, single notes on the negras, three notes to land on bar 70 (the user's example of page 10).

patterns.name: Melody in chords, one rhythm
patterns.line: The melody on top of three-note chords on every negra, with the same rhythm (corchea with puntillo, semicorchea, two negras) every two bars. Medium because every note is a chord, but the hand stays in one place, the rhythm repeats and the tempo is slow (it was hard before review 3).

patterns.name: Thirds and sixths in corcheas
patterns.line: Two notes on every corchea (Fa5-Reb5, Mib5-Sol4) after a long two-note chord. Medium because the notes are fast but the hand repeats one shape in one place (it was hard before review 3).

patterns.name: Full chords in octaves
patterns.line: Chords of four and five notes, ff, with the melody doubled at the octava and a jump up of an octava (La4-Do#5-La5, then La5-Do#6-La6), in negras and blancas. Medium because the chords are slow and are the usual chords of Mi and La with one or two altered notes; the jump is the only difficulty (it was super hard before review 4).

examples.piece: Ballade No. 1 in G minor, Op. 23

patterns.name: Broken chord over two octavas
patterns.line: Fa5-La5-Do6-Fa6-La6, then down: the notes of one chord in corcheas, going up two octavas and coming back. Medium because the hand must move, but it follows the same chord all the way.

patterns.name: A trill in thirds
patterns.line: Two thirds that rock in semicorcheas (Sol#-Si, then La-Do#), again and again. Medium at a moderate tempo because the hand never moves; Chopin asks for it very fast, which makes it an étude.

patterns.name: Two-note chords in a short-long rhythm
patterns.line: Thirds and sixths with a short note before a long one, the same figure every beat, with a few flats outside the armadura. Medium because of the rhythm and the alterations; the hand stays in one place.

patterns.name: Mazurka rhythm
patterns.line: A short note, then a long one on the same key, repeated, with a decoration note at the start. Medium because the rhythm is uneven, although the notes repeat.

patterns.name: Broken chord that keeps its shape
patterns.line: A broken chord in semicorcheas that is played again one step higher, with the same shape. Medium because it is fast and moves, but the fingers repeat one figure.

patterns.name: Two-note chords climbing
patterns.line: A melody in thirds and sixths in corcheas that climbs slowly, one note of the chord changing at a time. Medium because the hand moves up with a regular shape.

patterns.name: Melody with a decoration note
patterns.line: Long notes, each with one decoration note before it, and a few accidentals. Medium because of the decoration notes; the hand stays almost still.

examples.note: With a Sol# outside the armadura.

patterns.name: Quick run into a note
patterns.line: A few fast decoration notes that run up into a two-note chord, then a calm melody. Medium because the run is short and lands in the position of the melody.

patterns.name: Melody in thirds
patterns.line: Every note of the melody with the third under it, also on the corcheas. Medium because two fingers move together along the melody.

patterns.name: Melody landing on a chord
patterns.line: Single notes, and at the end of each phrase a chord of three notes of the harmony under the melody note. Medium because the chord comes only on the long, last notes.

patterns.name: Broken chord up and down in semicorcheas
patterns.line: Fa4-La4-Do5-Fa5-Do5-La4-Fa4-La4 at every half bar. Medium because it is fast and covers an octava, but the figure never changes.

patterns.name: Turn around the melody
patterns.line: Each negra of the melody played as four semicorcheas around it (the note, the step above, the note, the step below). Medium because it is fast, but it is the same turn every time.

patterns.name: Chromatic neighbour
patterns.line: Each negra of the melody comes from the semitone below (Sol#4-La4, Si4-Do5). Medium because of the small alterations, one per beat, in one position.

patterns.name: Melody with small pieces of chords
patterns.line: The melody on top (Sib5, Lab5, Solb5) with a second voice and two-note pieces of chords under it, and a few decoration notes. Hard because the hand plays the melody and part of the harmony (the brief's example of Ballade No. 4).

examples.piece: Ballade No. 4 in F minor, Op. 52

patterns.name: Melody over an inner line
patterns.line: The melody in negras with puntillo on the fifth finger, and a line of corcheas under it in the same hand. Hard because one hand plays two voices with different rhythms.

patterns.name: Runs in groups of 7 and 8
patterns.line: Runs of semicorcheas in groups of 7 and 8 over the left hand's sweeps. Hard because they are fast, but each group is mostly a chromatic scale with a small jump, which the hand plays with one fingering (it was super hard before review 4).

examples.piece: Ballade No. 4 in F minor, Op. 52

patterns.name: Scale run
patterns.line: A fast scale over two octavas or more, with the alterations of its key only. Hard because it is fast and the hand moves, but not super hard: a scale keeps one pattern and one fingering (the user's rule of review 4; it was medium before).

examples.note: A scale going down.

examples.piece: Ballade No. 1 in G minor, Op. 23
examples.note: The scale of Sol minor going up almost three octavas, with only Mi natural and Fa# (the melodic minor) outside the two flats. The app spells them Fab and Solb, its rule for the black and white keys under flats, so its drawing looks more chromatic than the edition.

patterns.name: Melody over a chromatic inner line
patterns.line: Two-note chords on top and, under them in the same hand, a line of semicorcheas that moves by semitones. Hard because one hand plays two voices fast, with many accidentals.

patterns.name: Thirds climbing by semitones
patterns.line: Thirds in corcheas that climb chromatically, with naturals and flats on almost every chord. Hard because the shape is regular but every chord is altered.

patterns.name: Chords moving in a run
patterns.line: Three-note chords in corcheas that go down one after the other, under an 8va line. Hard because the hand moves with full chords in the same run (the user's hard case).

patterns.name: Fast run without a fixed shape
patterns.line: A run of fusas and shorter notes that goes up and down with no repeated figure, after a decoration note. Hard because the fingers cannot repeat a shape.

examples.note: An ornament of the melody (fioritura) with accidentals.

patterns.name: Wide arpeggios with accidentals
patterns.line: Arpeggios in fusas over two octavas, with sharps outside the armadura; the shape repeats on each chord. Hard because the notes are very fast and the hand crosses a wide range.

patterns.name: Double notes climbing in a dotted rhythm
patterns.line: Two-note chords with a short note before a long one, climbing, with decoration notes and accidentals. Hard because the double notes move up while the rhythm stays uneven.

patterns.name: Double notes that jump
patterns.line: Two-note chords in corcheas that jump between positions, one after the other. Hard because each chord needs a new hand position.

patterns.name: Double notes in semicorcheas
patterns.line: Thirds and sixths in semicorcheas with naturals and flats, doubled by the left hand. Hard because the double notes are fast and change their alteration often.

patterns.name: Fast melody with many accidentals
patterns.line: A melody in semicorcheas with a few double notes, and naturals on many notes. Hard because the line is fast and keeps leaving the armadura.

patterns.name: Fast figure around a note
patterns.line: Semicorcheas that turn around one note with chromatic neighbours (a double sharp among them), against a left hand in another rhythm. Hard because of the speed and the alterations, although the figure repeats.

patterns.name: Chords climbing in corcheas
patterns.line: The triad moved one step up, three times, and back, in corcheas (Fa-La-Do, Sol-Sib-Re, La-Do-Mi, Sib-Re-Fa). Hard because full chords move in one run.

patterns.name: Sixths in semicorcheas
patterns.line: Sixths that go down by steps and back in semicorcheas. Hard because the hand plays double notes fast while it moves.

patterns.name: Melody in octavas
patterns.line: The melody doubled at the octava below. Hard because the hand stays open on the octava and jumps with every note.

patterns.name: Chromatic run
patterns.line: Eight semitones up from the top of the chord and back, in semicorcheas, with a sharp on every other note. Hard because it is fast and every note is altered.

patterns.name: Trill on long notes
patterns.line: The melody with a trill on its blanca. Hard because the trill asks for fast, even fingers while the melody goes on.

patterns.name: A line of irregular jumps
patterns.line: Corcheas that go up by jumps of different sizes, never by one tone or one semitone at a time (Sib3-Re4-Dob4-Re4-Do#4-Fa4-Re4-Lab4-Mi4-Lab4: up 4, down 3, up 3, down 1, up 4, down 3, up 6, down 4 semitones), with flats, naturals and sharps. Hard because the hand cannot follow a scale or a chord: each jump is a new distance, although the line keeps going up.

examples.piece: Ballade No. 1 in G minor, Op. 23
examples.note: The app spells Do# as Reb, Mi natural as Fab and Si natural as Dob (its rule under flats), so its drawing shows more flats than the edition.

patterns.name: Chords in semicorcheas going down
patterns.line: Three- and four-note chords in semicorcheas that go down by semitones, under an 8va line. Super hard because full chords move fast in one run.

patterns.name: Full chords that jump
patterns.line: Chords of three and four notes in corcheas that jump up and down, with a decoration note. Super hard because the hand opens and moves on every chord.

patterns.name: Double notes that change shape
patterns.line: Thirds, sixths and chords that change shape on every beat, with decoration notes, in Fa# major. Super hard because no shape repeats and the hand keeps moving.

patterns.name: Cadenza run
patterns.line: A run of very short notes down from Si6, outside the beat (a cadenza), which ends in two-note chords played at the same speed: Sol#4-Re#5 (a fifth), La#4-Do#5 (a third), Sol#4-La#4 (a second). Super hard because of those chords: their spacing changes from one chord to the next, so the hand cannot keep one shape, inside a fast run that goes down. The range is not the reason: the run itself uses only the notes of Si major, and a fast scale of the key over many octavas is easy to hard.

patterns.name: Very fast wide zig-zag
patterns.line: Fusas that jump up and down in a wide zig-zag after a few chords. Super hard because each note is far from the one before, at a high speed.

patterns.name: Jumps with fast figures
patterns.line: A low note, then a fast figure an octava or more higher, again and again, with sharps. Super hard because the hand jumps and plays fast at each landing.

patterns.name: Octavas in semicorcheas
patterns.line: A scale in octavas going up and down in semicorcheas. Super hard because the open hand moves fast.

patterns.name: Chords jumping an octava
patterns.line: A four-note chord, then the same chord an octava higher, again and again in corcheas. Super hard because the hand jumps with a full chord on every note.

patterns.name: Chromatic thirds
patterns.line: Thirds that go up and down by semitones in semicorcheas. Super hard because two fingers play a fast chromatic line together.

patterns.name: Octava frames that break their pattern
patterns.line: Fast corcheas in groups of six: an octava (Do4-Do5), two notes inside it (Fa4, La4), then a frame that is not an octava (Mi4 natural to Reb5), and the next group again different (Fa#4 to Mib5); the figure moves up a step every half bar, over an inner voice held in negras, with naturals, sharps and flats. Super hard because the pattern starts and then breaks: the hand opens an octava, then a different distance, so it cannot keep one shape while it plays fast.

examples.piece: Ballade No. 1 in G minor, Op. 23
examples.note: The app spells Do# as Reb, Mi natural as Fab and Si natural as Dob (its rule under flats), so its drawing shows more flats than the edition. The held negras of the inner voice are written as corcheas (one voice per hand).

patterns.name: A melody over its own inner semicorcheas
patterns.line: Two voices in the right hand. On top, the melody in corcheas (stems up, fingers 4 and 5); under it, a line of semicorcheas (stems down, thumb and fingers 1 to 3) that fills the time between two melody notes, so that the melody sounds continuous. The inner line adds no new voice: it walks between the notes of the chord while the melody waits. Where both voices meet on a beat the hand plays a chord, between the beats a single note. Naturals come and go (Mi natural, La natural, Solb). Super hard because one hand plays two voices with different fingers and different weight, the melody held and sung, the inner line soft and even, while the left hand plays its own jumps and arpeggios.

examples.piece: Ballade No. 4 in F minor, Op. 52
examples.note: The app draws one voice per hand: the melody (stems up) and the inner notes (stems down) become one line of chords and single notes, so the two voices of the edition are not visible in the drawing. The app spells Mi natural as Fab (its rule under flats).

examples.piece: Ballade No. 4 in F minor, Op. 52
examples.note: The app draws one voice per hand: the melody (stems up) and the inner notes (stems down) become one line of chords and single notes, so the two voices of the edition are not visible in the drawing.

patterns.name: Chords with single notes between them
patterns.line: The melody moves in octavas or chords on the beats (Do4-Do5, Mib4-Mib5, Solb4-Solb5), and between two of them the hand plays single notes (Sib4, Lab4, Sol4; Mib5, Fa5, Reb5, Do5, Sib4) that keep the pulse going while the melody waits for its next note. The single notes are accompaniment played by the right hand, not a new voice. Super hard because the hand opens to an octava or a chord and closes to one note at speed, again and again, with the melody on the top finger, while the left hand is busy.

examples.piece: Ballade No. 4 in F minor, Op. 52
examples.note: The app draws one voice per hand: the melody (stems up) and the inner notes (stems down) become one line of chords and single notes, so the two voices of the edition are not visible in the drawing.

examples.piece: Ballade No. 4 in F minor, Op. 52
examples.note: The app draws one voice per hand: the melody (stems up) and the inner notes (stems down) become one line of chords and single notes, so the two voices of the edition are not visible in the drawing. Both kern editions differ from this edition in the second half of the bar; the drawing follows the edition: Mib4 over a held La natural 4, and the rising notes Do4-Mib4-Solb4-Fa4 in the left hand.

patterns.name: Thirds going down and up, now and then three notes
patterns.line: Thirds in semicorcheas (Reb5-Fab5, Do5-Mib5, Sib4-Reb5, Lab4-Do5, Sol4-Sib4) that go down and come back up under a melody in corcheas (Sol5, Reb5, Fab5, Mib5), and from time to time a chord of three notes (Mib4-Lab4-Do5) or a wider one (Mib4-Reb5). Super hard because two fingers play fast thirds while the top finger holds and stresses the melody, the hand changes shape each time a third note joins, and Fab5 then Fa natural 5 come in the same bar.

examples.piece: Ballade No. 4 in F minor, Op. 52
examples.note: The app draws one voice per hand: the melody (stems up) and the inner notes (stems down) become one line of chords and single notes, so the two voices of the edition are not visible in the drawing.

examples.piece: Ballade No. 4 in F minor, Op. 52
examples.note: The app draws one voice per hand: the melody (stems up) and the inner notes (stems down) become one line of chords and single notes, so the two voices of the edition are not visible in the drawing. The edition writes a becuadro on the Fa5 after the Fab5 of the same bar; the app draws no bars and prints a sign only on notes outside the armadura, so its Fa5 has no sign (it is still Fa natural).

patterns.name: Held triad
patterns.line: The chord of the harmony (Fa-La-Do) held under the melody; the hand changes position only when the harmony changes. Easy because the hand holds one shape and does not move inside the chord.

examples.piece: From the brief, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Low note, then the chord
patterns.line: Fa2, then Fa3-La3-Do4: one note and one chord, the same shape every time. Easy because the hand makes one jump of an octave to a triad that does not change.

examples.piece: From the brief, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Triads in steps
patterns.line: The triad slides one step up or down with the melody (Fa-La-Do, Sol-Sib-Re, La-Do-Mi). Easy because the three fingers keep one shape and the hand moves one key at a time.

examples.piece: From the brief, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Held chord, repeated
patterns.line: A small chord held as a blanca and played again with the same notes, bar after bar. Easy because the hand does not move at all.

examples.piece: Ballade No. 1 in G minor, Op. 23

patterns.name: Low note, then two notes rocking
patterns.line: Fa2, then La3-Do4-La3-Do4 in corcheas: one low note, then two notes of the chord one after the other. Easy because after the low note the hand stays on two keys.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Alberti bass
patterns.line: Fa3-Do4-La3-Do4 in corcheas, again and again: the lowest, the highest and the middle note of the triad. Easy because the hand never leaves the position of the triad.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Triad up and down
patterns.line: Fa3-La3-Do4-La3 in corcheas: the three notes of the chord going up and coming down. Easy because the figure is symmetric and stays in one position.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Triad up, then held
patterns.line: Fa3 and La3 in corcheas, then Do4 as a negra: the triad goes up and stops on its top note. Easy because three fingers stay on three keys.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Triad down, then held
patterns.line: Do4 and La3 in corcheas, then Fa3 as a negra: the same figure going down. Easy for the same reason as going up.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Chord, then two notes above
patterns.line: Fa3-La3-Do4, then Do4-Fa4: the chord, then two of its notes in a higher position, again and again. Easy because the hand moves a little and comes back, always with the same two shapes.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Held two-note chord
patterns.line: The fifth Fa3-Do4 held as blancas (Do3-Sol3 and Sib2-Fa3 for the other chords). Easy because two notes are enough to give the harmony and the hand holds one shape.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Low note, then two-note chords
patterns.line: Fa2, then La3-Do4 three times in negras. Easy because the chord has only two notes and its shape never changes.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Two-note chord, then an arpeggio
patterns.line: Fa3-Do4 together, then Fa3-La3-Do4-La3-Fa3-La3 in corcheas. Easy because the arpeggio uses the same position as the two-note chord.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Fifth to sixth, rocking
patterns.line: Fa3-Do4, then Fa3-Re4, in negras: the upper note moves one key and back while the lower note stays. Easy because only one finger moves.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Low note, then the octave
patterns.line: Mi2, then the octave Mi3-Mi4 on the two next beats, in a slow tempo. Medium because of the octava; the jump and the shape are the same in every bar.

patterns.name: Low note, then two chords
patterns.line: The waltz left hand: a low note on the first beat, then the same chord on the second and third beats. Medium because the hand jumps every bar, but the chord shape stays and only the bass note changes.

examples.note: Si2, then Fa#3-Si3-Re4 twice: the plain pattern.
Lab2, Mib2, Lab2 under the same chord Mib3-Lab3-Do4: only the fifth finger moves.
Do#2, then Sol#3-Do#4-Mi4: the same pattern with a jump of more than an octave, the hardest form of it.

patterns.name: Held bass under two chords
patterns.line: The low note is held for the whole bar (blanca with puntillo) while two chords sound on the second and third beats. Medium because there is no jump: the hand stays over the bass and the chord.

patterns.name: Low note, then two chords, in corcheas
patterns.line: Mib2, then two chords in beamed corcheas (Sol3-Mib4, then Sib3-Mib4-Sol4), three times in a bar. Medium because the figure repeats at every beat; the second chord only adds a note on top.

patterns.name: Same chord, one note changes
patterns.line: One chord repeated in corcheas (Sol3-Si3-Mi4); every bar or half bar one or two of its notes move down (Fa#3-La3-Mi4, then Fa#3-La3-Mib4, then Fa3-La3-Mib4). Medium because of the many notes, but the hand never leaves its position.

patterns.name: Repeated note
patterns.line: Lab3 repeated in corcheas, with a low note and a small chord on the strong beats. Medium because the thumb stays on one key and the other fingers add the harmony.

patterns.name: Octave bass in negras
patterns.line: Octavas in negras that walk down by semitones (Do, Si, Sib, La, Lab, Sol). Medium because the hand keeps the octave shape and slides; it gives a strong bass without more notes.

patterns.name: Low note, then a small wave
patterns.line: Fa#2, then Mi#3-Sol#3-Fa#3-La#3 and back to Do#3: a low note and a short figure up and down inside one hand position, the same at every half bar. Medium because the figure never changes.

patterns.name: Simple line in negras
patterns.line: Single notes in negras: a low note, then a broken chord that climbs, with a step or two between its notes (Sib1, Sib2, Lab3, Fa3, Do4, Sib3). Medium because there are few notes and they are easy to read, although they belong to no fixed shape (the user's example of page 10).

examples.piece: Ballade No. 1 in G minor, Op. 23

patterns.name: Octava, then an arpeggio
patterns.line: Fa2-Fa3 together, then Fa3-La3-Do4-La3-Fa3-La3 in corcheas. Medium because of the octava and the jump to the arpeggio; the arpeggio itself stays in one position.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Low note, then chords off the beat
patterns.line: Fa2 on the beat, then the triad on the half beats (corcheas), with blank space between them. Medium because of the rhythm: the chord sounds between the beats.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Added sixth, up and down
patterns.line: Fa3-La3-Do4-Re4 and back in corcheas: the triad with its sixth (Re), a new note of the chord. Medium because the hand uses four fingers, still in one position.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Held bass under rocking notes
patterns.line: Fa3 held for the whole bar while La3-Do4 rock above it in corcheas. Medium because one hand plays two voices: one finger holds and the others move.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Triad in semicorcheas
patterns.line: Fa3-La3-Do4-La3 in semicorcheas at every beat. Medium because the notes are fast, although the figure and the position never change.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Octava, then two beamed chords
patterns.line: Fa2-Fa3, then the triad twice in beamed corcheas, twice in each bar (the brief's example of an octava and two corcheas of the chord). Medium because of the jump between the octava and the chord.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Alternating bass and chord
patterns.line: Fa2, the triad, Do3, the triad, in negras: the bass changes between the root and the fifth of the chord. Medium because the bass note moves every two beats.

examples.piece: A variation asked in the review of 2026-10-29, drawn by the app

patterns.name: Arpeggio in 3 + 3 + 2
patterns.line: The triad in corcheas grouped 3 + 3 + 2 (Fa3-La3-Do4, Fa3-La3-Do4, Fa3-La3), a common rhythm in pop songs. Medium because the groups do not follow the beat, although the notes stay in one position.

patterns.name: Octavas rocking
patterns.line: Fa2, Fa3, Fa2, Fa3 in corcheas: the octava played as two notes, one after the other. Medium because the hand stays open on the octava for the whole bar.

patterns.name: Chord, then an arpeggio down
patterns.line: The triad, then Fa4-Do4-La3-Fa3-La3-Do4 in corcheas: down from the top and back. Medium because the arpeggio covers an octava, one note more than the triad.

patterns.name: Octave, then the chord up and down
patterns.line: The octava Mi1-Mi2, then the chord in negras going up and coming down with the same notes. Hard because the hand jumps and changes fingers, but the way down repeats the way up (the user's example of page 12).

examples.piece: Ballade No. 1 in G minor, Op. 23

patterns.name: Low note, then a chord that moves
patterns.line: Fa3, then Reb4-Mi4-Sol4 and the same shape one step lower (Sib3-Reb4-Mi4); then Fa2, Do4-Fa4-Lab4 and Lab3-Do4-Fa4. Hard because the second chord moves (the brief's hard level) and the hand crosses from the bass to the treble clef.

patterns.name: Octaves that draw the chord
patterns.line: Octavas in corcheas that go through the notes of the chord (Solb, Reb, Solb, Sib, Mib, Sib) under held chords of the right hand. Hard because the hand moves on every note, but it keeps the octave shape and a regular figure.

examples.piece: Ballade No. 4 in F minor, Op. 52

patterns.name: Wave in one position
patterns.line: A low note, then semicorcheas in groups of six that go up and come down over the chord (Dob2, then Dob3-Reb3-Fa3-Reb4-Fa3-Reb3). Hard because they are fast, but each wave is symmetric and the hand stays over one place.

patterns.name: A line that belongs to no chord
patterns.line: A low note, then two-note chords in corcheas whose notes move apart, the lower one down by semitones and the upper one up (Mi3-Sol3, Mib3-La3, Re3-Sib3, Do3-Do4). Hard because the line fits no known chord (the brief's irregular passages), but the hand stays in one position.

patterns.name: Four-note arpeggio up and down
patterns.line: Fa3-La3-Do4-Fa4 and back in corcheas: the triad with its octava as a fourth note. Hard because the hand is open on the octava and uses all five fingers.

patterns.name: Low note, then four-note chords
patterns.line: Fa2, then Fa3-La3-Do4-Fa4 three times in negras. Hard because the chord fills the octava and the hand jumps to it.

patterns.name: Open arpeggio up and down
patterns.line: Fa2-Do3-Fa3-La3-Do4 and back in corcheas: the root, the fifth, the octava and the tenth. Hard because the arpeggio covers more than an octava and the hand must move inside it.

patterns.name: Alberti over an octava
patterns.line: Fa3-Fa4-Do4-Fa4, La3-Fa4-Do4-Fa4: the Alberti figure with the octava on top. Hard because the hand stays open on the octava while the lower fingers change.

patterns.name: Four-note wave in semicorcheas
patterns.line: Fa2, then Fa3-La3-Do4-Fa4 up and down in semicorcheas. Hard because the wave is fast and covers an octava; it is symmetric, so the fingers repeat.

patterns.line: Fa2-Fa3, then Fa3-La3-Do4 and La3-Do4-Fa4 in corcheas: the second chord is the same chord one position higher (the brief's La4-Do5-Mi5, then Do5-Mi5-La5). Hard because the hand moves between the two chords.

patterns.name: Octava, then four-note chords
patterns.line: Fa2-Fa3, then Fa3-La3-Do4-Fa4 six times in corcheas. Hard because the hand jumps and then repeats a full chord fast.

patterns.name: Held bass under moving thirds
patterns.line: Fa3 held, with La3-Do4 and Sib3-Re4 moving above it in corcheas. Hard because one hand plays two voices and the upper voice moves two fingers at a time.

patterns.name: Four-note chords off the beat
patterns.line: Fa2-Fa3 on the beat, then Fa3-La3-Do4-Fa4 on the half beats. Hard because of the jump, the full chord and the rhythm between the beats.

patterns.name: Arpeggio up, then the chord
patterns.line: Fa3-La3-Do4-Fa4 in corcheas, then the four notes together as a blanca. Hard because the hand covers the octava twice, first note by note and then all at once.

patterns.name: Broken octava, then the chord around its upper note
patterns.line: Sol2, then Sol3 (the octava played as two notes), and the hand stays up there: Fa3-Si3 together, Sol3, Mi3, Sol3, in semicorcheas; then Do3, Sol3, Do4, La3, Sol3. Hard because it is fast and the hand jumps an octava at every half bar, but after the jump all the notes are in reach: the thumb comes back to the upper note (Sol3) and the other fingers play the chord around it.

examples.piece: Ballade No. 4 in F minor, Op. 52
examples.note: The app writes Mi natural as Fab and Si natural as Dob (its rule: a white key whose name is in the armadura takes its other name), so Fa3-Si3 is drawn Fa3-Dob4.

patterns.name: Low note, then a line with a passing note
patterns.line: Do2, then Sol3, Do4, Re4, Mi4 in semicorcheas up to a corchea: after the jump the hand climbs the chord (Sol, Do, Mi) with Re as a passing note between Do and Mi, so it is not a plain arpeggio. Hard because of the jump of more than an octava and the speed; the notes after the jump are next to each other, with no other jump (first half of the bar).

examples.piece: Ballade No. 4 in F minor, Op. 52
examples.note: The app writes Mi natural as Fab (its rule: a white key whose name is in the armadura takes its other name).

patterns.name: A note the thumb comes back to, with a reach below
patterns.line: Fa2, then Do4, La3, Do4, Re3, Do4 in semicorcheas: the thumb comes back to Do4 again and again, and the other notes are around it; Re3, ten semitones below, is reached by the fifth finger without moving the hand. Hard because it is fast and the hand is open almost an octava, but it stays in one position after the low note (second half of the bar; the same figure ends bar 2).

patterns.name: Sweeps over two octaves
patterns.line: From Fa2 up to Lab4 in six semicorcheas, twice in each bar, then a jump back down. Super hard because the hand opens, crosses and jumps without rest while the right hand runs in groups of 7 and 8.

examples.piece: Ballade No. 4 in F minor, Op. 52

patterns.name: Fast octaves in stretto
patterns.line: A chord, then octavas in corcheas (Dob, Sib, Do, Sib), faster and faster (stretto), under chords of four notes that jump in the right hand. Super hard because both hands play heavy shapes at speed.
